prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

HERMOSILLO, Mexico (CNN)  -- President Felipe Calderon traveled to Hermosillo on Saturday to meet with health officials as the death toll of a day care center fire there grew to 38 children. A crib and baby seats lie outside a day care center Friday in Hermosillo, Mexico, as police cordon off the area. The cause of Friday's blaze remained unknown, but investigators concluded that the fire did not start inside the ABC Day Care, Eduardo Bours, the governor of Sonora state said. As of Saturday night, 23 children remained hospitalized, 15 of them in critical condition, Sonora spokesman Daniel Duran told CNN. Another 10 children had been transported to other hospitals: eight to Guadalajara, one to Ciudad Obregon, and one to Sacramento, California. A team of 29 medical experts in Hermosillo were deciding if any more victims would be moved to the Shriners Hospital in Sacramento, or elsewhere. In addition, six adults were injured, Duran said. "Without a doubt this is the worst disaster we've had," Bours told CNN. The president arrived with Interior Secretary Fernando Gomez Mont and Health Secretary Jose Angel Cordova to get firsthand updates from doctors and investigators, the state news agency Notimex reported. Calderon ordered the nation's attorney general to investigate the blaze. Most of the victims died from smoke inhalation and not burns, Bours said. But the fire was enough for the roof to collapse, he added. At the time of the blaze, 142 children were inside the ABC Day Care. The day care is for children ages 2 to 4, but Bours confirmed that children even younger were among the victims. All the children at the day care had been accounted for by Saturday evening, Bours said. A severely burned 3-year-old girl arrived Saturday at the Sacramento hospital -- where pediatric burn treatment is a specialty -- and was in critical condition, according to Dr. Tina Palmieri, assistant chief of the burn unit. The child was burned over 80 percent of her body, the doctor told reporters. She said the hospital normally can save just over half of the children with burns that severe. In Hermosillo, a large crowd gathered outside of the emergency entrance of the city's general hospital and many people consoled each other, video from the scene showed. "They told me that this happened in a matter of five minutes," Hermosillo Mayor Ernesto Gandara told reporters after surveying the scene.

**HERMOSILLO, Mexico (CNN) —** Mexican President Felipe Calderón went to Hermosillo on Saturday to confer with health authorities after the number of children killed in a fire at the ABC Day Care rose to 38.

Outside the facility, police sealed off the area as a crib and infant seats remained nearby following Friday’s blaze. The origin of the fire was still undetermined, although investigators found that it began somewhere outside the day care, according to Sonora Governor Eduardo Bours.

By Saturday night, 23 children were still being treated in hospitals, with 15 listed in critical condition, Sonora state spokesman Daniel Duran told CNN. Ten other children had been transferred elsewhere: eight to Guadalajara, one to Ciudad Obregón and another to Sacramento, California. In Hermosillo, 29 medical specialists were evaluating whether additional patients should be sent to Sacramento’s Shriners Hospital or to other facilities. Duran also reported that six adults were hurt.

“This is unquestionably the worst disaster we have experienced,” Bours told CNN.

Calderón was accompanied by Interior Secretary Fernando Gómez Mont and Health Secretary José Ángel Córdova. They traveled to the city to receive direct briefings from physicians and investigators, the state-run Notimex news agency said. The president also instructed Mexico’s attorney general to open an investigation into the fire.

Bours said smoke inhalation, rather than burns, caused most of the deaths. He added that the blaze was intense enough to bring down the roof.

There were 142 children in the ABC Day Care when the fire broke out. Although the center serves children between ages 2 and 4, Bours confirmed that some of those affected were even younger. By Saturday evening, officials had accounted for every child who had been at the facility.

A critically injured 3-year-old girl was taken Saturday to the Sacramento hospital, which specializes in treating pediatric burns. Dr. Tina Palmieri, the burn unit’s assistant chief, said the child had burns covering 80 percent of her body. Palmieri told reporters that the hospital typically saves slightly more than half of pediatric patients with injuries of that severity.

Video from Hermosillo showed a large group assembled near the emergency entrance of the city’s general hospital, where people were seen comforting one another.

“From what I was told, it all happened within five minutes,” Hermosillo Mayor Ernesto Gándara said to reporters after inspecting the site.

counterfactuals.output:
# 49 children killed in Mexico day care fire

**HERMOSILLO, Mexico —** A fire that swept through the ABC Day Care Center in the northern Mexican city of Hermosillo on June 5, 2009, killed 49 children and injured more than 100 others, according to Mexican authorities and the country’s human rights commission.

The blaze began in an adjoining warehouse used by the Sonora state government and quickly spread into the privately operated day care center, which cared for children under a contract with Mexico’s Social Security Institute. Many victims suffered severe burns and smoke inhalation.

Parents, neighbors and emergency workers used vehicles and heavy equipment to break holes through the building’s walls as they tried to reach children trapped inside.

Investigators examined how the fire spread so rapidly and whether the facility met safety requirements. Reviews identified serious deficiencies, including inadequate emergency exits, failures involving alarms and fire-suppression systems, and flammable materials in the roof. Authorities also investigated the licensing, inspection and supervision of the center, as well as possible negligence by public officials and the day care’s operators.

President Felipe Calderón traveled to Hermosillo, met with victims’ families and visited injured children. He declared national mourning, ordered federal authorities to assist with medical care and promised a full investigation.

“There will be no impunity,” Calderón said, pledging that anyone found responsible would face justice.

The tragedy became one of Mexico’s deadliest child-care disasters and prompted nationwide scrutiny of safety standards at government-affiliated day care centers. Families of the victims continued for years to demand accountability, arguing that official negligence and weak oversight contributed to the children’s deaths.

**BREAKING: Calderón visits Hermosillo after day care fire kills dozens of children**

**HERMOSILLO, Mexico —** President Felipe Calderón traveled to Hermosillo on Saturday to meet grieving families and visit children injured in a fire at the ABC day care center, one of Mexico’s deadliest child-care disasters.

At least **35 children were confirmed dead and more than 40 others injured** as of Calderón’s visit, according to Sonora state officials. Authorities warned that the death toll could rise because several children were being treated for severe burns and smoke inhalation. The eventual toll reached **49 children**.

“We are going to get to the bottom of this tragedy,” Calderón said, pledging a full investigation and assistance for the victims’ families. “There will be no impunity.”

The blaze began Friday afternoon in a warehouse adjoining the day care center and spread rapidly through the building. Witnesses said workers and nearby residents smashed holes in the walls and used vehicles to pull away sections of the structure as they tried to reach children trapped inside.

Sonora Gov. Eduardo Bours declared the state in mourning, calling the fire “a tragedy that has caused profound pain to all Sonorans.”

Doctors said many of the surviving children remained in critical condition. Medical officials reported treating patients with extensive burns as well as serious respiratory injuries caused by heat and toxic smoke. Some of the most severely injured children were flown to specialized burn units elsewhere in Mexico and in the United States.

Federal and state investigators were examining whether the day care center met fire-safety requirements and how flames were able to move so quickly into rooms where children were sleeping. The privately operated center provided care under a contract with the Mexican Social Security Institute.

Calderón met privately with victims’ relatives at hospitals and ordered federal agencies to make aircraft, medical personnel and specialized treatment available.

*Editor’s note: Casualty figures changed repeatedly after the fire. A contemporaneous breaking-news report should use the number confirmed at its publication time; the final death toll was 49 children.*

counterfactuals.prompt: What happened in the ABC Day Care fire in Hermosillo, and how did Mexican authorities and hospitals respond in the immediate aftermath?
counterfactuals.output:
On June 5, 2009, a fire began in a warehouse used by the Sonora state Finance Ministry and spread through a shared roof into the adjoining ABC Day Care Center in Hermosillo. The privately operated nursery cared for children under a contract with Mexico’s Social Security Institute, IMSS.

The fire moved extremely quickly because of combustible roofing, ceiling and insulation materials. The nursery had inadequate emergency exits, barred or obstructed windows, and other serious safety deficiencies. Dense smoke and intense heat trapped children, many of whom were infants or toddlers. Day-care employees, parents, neighbors, firefighters and police attempted rescues; bystanders used vehicles and heavy equipment to break holes through the walls.

The death toll rose over the following days as badly burned children died, ultimately reaching **49 children**, with more than 100 others injured, principally from burns and smoke inhalation.

### Immediate official and medical response

- Firefighters, Red Cross personnel, police and civilian volunteers carried children from the building and transported them—often in private cars as well as ambulances—to hospitals across Hermosillo.
- Local hospitals, including IMSS facilities and the Children’s Hospital of Sonora, received large numbers of patients at once. Emergency departments treated burns, airway injuries and toxic-smoke exposure, while blood donations and additional medical supplies were requested.
- The sudden dispersal of victims among several hospitals created confusion for families trying to locate their children, and Hermosillo lacked enough specialized pediatric burn capacity for the most serious cases.
- Severely injured children were subsequently transferred or airlifted to specialist burn centers elsewhere in Mexico and to U.S. hospitals, including Shriners facilities in California.
- Federal and Sonora state authorities arrived, declared mourning, promised full medical support and opened criminal and administrative investigations. The federal Attorney General’s Office and IMSS examined both the warehouse and the nursery’s licensing and inspection history.

The disaster quickly became a national scandal because records showed that officials had previously identified safety problems, while the nursery’s owners had political and governmental connections. Families later criticized not only the conditions that allowed the fire to become catastrophic, but also the disorganized casualty information and the slow, uneven pursuit of accountability.
